subject: Biology
title: C3, C4, and CAM Plants
description: A quick, practical guide to C3, C4, and CAM Plants.

hook.text: Not all plants photosynthesize the same way. Some evolved clever tricks to handle heat and drought.

buildup.text: C3 plants use the standard Calvin cycle. They thrive in cool, moist climates.

discovery.text: C4 plants like corn pre-concentrate CO₂, reducing water loss in hot sunny environments.

twist.text: CAM plants like cacti open stomata only at night to save water, storing CO₂ for daytime use.

climax.text: These adaptations let plants colonize deserts, tropics, and grasslands that C3 plants can't handle.

punchline.text: Same goal, three strategies. Plants adapt or die.

quiz.question: When do CAM plants open their stomata?

details.summary: Plants use three photosynthetic pathways. C3 plants fix carbon directly but lose water and efficiency in heat. C4 plants concentrate CO2 to avoid this loss. CAM plants open stomata only at night to conserve water, allowing them to thrive in the driest environments on Earth.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding photosynthetic pathways explains why certain crops grow better in specific climates. Engineering C4 traits into C3 crops like rice could dramatically increase yields in a warming world with growing food demand.
takeaways: C3 plants like wheat and rice fix carbon directly but lose efficiency in hot conditions
C4 plants like corn and sugarcane concentrate CO2 for higher efficiency in heat
CAM plants like cacti fix CO2 at night to minimize water loss in deserts

faq.question: Why are C4 plants more efficient in hot climates?
faq.answer: In hot conditions, C3 plants lose CO2 through photorespiration when oxygen competes with CO2. C4 plants avoid this by concentrating CO2 in specialized cells before fixation, maintaining high efficiency even when stomata partially close in heat.

faq.question: How do CAM plants survive in deserts?
faq.answer: CAM plants open their stomata only at night when temperatures are cool and humidity higher, taking in CO2 with minimal water loss. They store the CO2 as organic acids overnight, then use it for photosynthesis during the day with stomata closed.
